questions.problem:
Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡u=\frac{3}{5},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v=\frac{8}{17},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡v=-\frac{15}{17}.
$$

Given that $u$ lies in the first quadrant, find the value of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, recall the difference formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{sin}⁡v$, and $\operatorname{cos}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡u+{cos}^{2}⁡u=1\,⟹\,{cos}^{2}⁡u=1-{sin}^{2}⁡u
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡u & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡u \\  & =1-{(\frac{3}{5})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{{3}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{9}{25} \\  & =\frac{25}{25}-\frac{9}{25} \\  & =\frac{16}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡u & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{16}{25}} \\  & =\pm \frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $u$ lies in the first quadrant, where cosine is positive. So, we disregard the negative value, and we have 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡u=\frac{4}{5}.
$$

We can now apply the difference formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(\frac{3}{5})(-\frac{15}{17})-(\frac{4}{5})(\frac{8}{17}) \\  & =-\frac{45}{85}-\frac{32}{85} \\  & =-\frac{77}{85}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡u=\frac{3}{5},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡u=-\frac{4}{5},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡v=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

If $v$ lies in the first quadrant, then $\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, and $\operatorname{cos}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{sin}⁡v$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡v+{cos}^{2}⁡v=1\,⟹\,{sin}^{2}⁡v=1-{cos}^{2}⁡v
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡v & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡v \\  & =1-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{4}{4}-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $v$ lies in the first quadrant, where sine is positive. So, we disregard the negative value, and we have 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡v=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.
$$

We can now apply the sum formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(\frac{3}{5})(\frac{1}{2})+(-\frac{4}{5})(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{3}{10}-\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{10} \\  & =\frac{3-4\sqrt{3}}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡u=\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v=\frac{2}{7},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡v=-\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7}.
$$

Given that $u$ lies in the first quadrant, and

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\frac{a-b\sqrt{55}}{42},
$$

calculate the value of $a+b.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{sin}⁡v$, and $\operatorname{cos}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡u+{cos}^{2}⁡u=1\,⟹\,{cos}^{2}⁡u=1-{sin}^{2}⁡u
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡u & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡u \\  & =1-{(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{(\sqrt{11})^{2}}{{6}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{11}{36} \\  & =\frac{36}{36}-\frac{11}{36} \\  & =\frac{36-11}{36} \\  & =\frac{25}{36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡u & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{25}{36}} \\  & =\pm \frac{5}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $u$ lies in the first quadrant, where cosine is positive. So, we disregard the negative value, and we have 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡u=\frac{5}{6}.
$$

We can now apply the sum formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6})(-\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7})+(\frac{5}{6})(\frac{2}{7}) \\  & =-\frac{3\sqrt{55}}{42}+\frac{10}{42} \\  & =\frac{10-3\sqrt{55}}{42}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a=10,b=3,$ and $a+b=13.$

questions.problem:
Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡u=-\frac{\sqrt{5}}{4},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡u=\frac{\sqrt{11}}{4},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡v=-\frac{5}{6}.
$$

Given that $v$ lies in the second quadrant, and

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)=\frac{a\sqrt{5}-b}{24},
$$

calculate the value of $a+b.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, recall the difference formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, and $\operatorname{cos}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{sin}⁡v$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡v+{cos}^{2}⁡v=1\,⟹\,{sin}^{2}⁡v=1-{cos}^{2}⁡v
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡v & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡v \\  & =1-{(-\frac{5}{6})}^{2} \\  & =1-{(\frac{5}{6})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{{5}^{2}}{{6}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{25}{36} \\  & =\frac{36}{36}-\frac{25}{36} \\  & =\frac{11}{36}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{11}{36}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{11}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $v$ lies in the second quadrant, where sine is positive. So, we disregard the negative value, and we have 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡v=\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6}.
$$

We can now apply the difference formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(-\frac{\sqrt{5}}{4})(-\frac{5}{6})-(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{4})(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6}) \\  & =\frac{5\sqrt{5}}{24}-\frac{11}{24} \\  & =\frac{5\sqrt{5}-11}{24}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a=5,b=11,$ and $a+b=16.$

canonical_examples.problem:
Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\sin u = \dfrac{3}{4}, \qquad \cos u =  -\dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{4}, \qquad \cos v = \dfrac{4}{5}.
$$

Given that $v$ lies in the first quadrant, and

$$
\sin\left(u + v\right) = \dfrac{a- b\sqrt 7}{20},
$$

calculate the value of $a+b.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\sin(u+v) = \sin u \cos v+ \cos u \sin v
$$

We know the values of $\sin{u},$ $\cos{u},$ and $\cos{v}.$ To find the missing value of $\sin{v},$ we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\sin^2 v + \cos^2 v= 1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \sin^2 v = 1- \cos^2 v
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡v & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡v \\  & =1-{(\frac{4}{5})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{{4}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{16}{25} \\  & =\frac{25}{25}-\frac{16}{25} \\  & =\frac{25-16}{25} \\  & =\frac{9}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{9}{25}} \\  & =\pm \frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $v$ lies in the first quadrant, where sine is positive. So, we disregard the negative value, and we have 

$$
\sin v= \dfrac{3}{5}.
$$

We can now apply the sum formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(\frac{3}{4})(\frac{4}{5})+(-\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4})(\frac{3}{5}) \\  & =\frac{12}{20}-\frac{3\sqrt{7}}{20} \\  & =\frac{12-3\sqrt{7}}{20}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a=12, b=3,$ and $a+b = 15.$

\sin(u-v) = \sin u \cos v- \cos u \sin v
$$

We know the values of $\cos{u}$, $\sin{v}$, and $\cos{v}.$ To find the missing value of $\sin{u}$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\sin^2 u + \cos^2 u= 1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \sin^2 u = 1- \cos^2 u
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡u & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡u \\  & =1-{(\frac{7}{25})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{{7}^{2}}{{25}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{49}{625} \\  & =\frac{625}{625}-\frac{49}{625} \\  & =\frac{576}{625}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡u & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{576}{625}} \\  & =\pm \frac{24}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $u$ lies in the fourth quadrant, where sine is negative. So, we disregard the positive value, and we have 

$$
\sin u= -\dfrac{24}{25}.
$$

We can now apply the difference formula, as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
		\sin(u - v) 
			&= \sin u \cos v - \cos u \sin v \[5pt]
			&= \left( -\dfrac {24}{25} \right)\left(\dfrac {3} {5}\right)
 				 -  \left(\dfrac {7}{25}\right) \left( \dfrac {4} {5}\right) \[5pt]
			
 			&= -\dfrac {72} {125} -  \dfrac {28} {125} \[5pt]
			&= -\dfrac {100} {125}\[5pt]
			&= -\dfrac {4} {5}.
	}
$$
